Pele Yoetz 97:2: And it is known that the books of Questions and Responsa produced in every generation have served as our eyes. And Israel is not widowed - it is fitting for whoever the LORD has graced with understanding to clarify the law he has entered into the house of doubt about, and to examine well the Gemara and the halachic authorities, until halachah emerges as clear as a garment, resting upon commentators' explicit words. And let it be written in a book only what pertains to the legal matter, and let him not mix the work of a Talmudic commentary [pilpul] with the work of a responsum, and thereby it shall be of benefit to the many for future generations. And in any case, one should not rely on everything found written, until he examines it by the standard of his own true reasoning, for every man is a liar, and "according to the difficulty is the error" (Bava Metzia 96b). And there are laws that are like mountains hanging by a hair (see Chagigah 10b), where a small distinction changes the law - and this responsibility rests upon those who sit in judgment, that they be sharp to understand the depth of the law and to easily compare one case to another, and let them seek mercy regarding this secret, that God grace them with wisdom, knowledge, and understanding.
Pele Yoetz 98:1: Power of Attorney - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shevuot 31a): "and he who has not done good among his people" (Ezekiel 18:18) - this refers to one who comes with a power of attorney [to litigate on another's behalf], for he crosses over and involves himself in a quarrel not his own. And there are already grounds for permitting this, as explained by the halachic authorities, but the complete man, who loves peace and pursues peace, shall not wish to enter this fray for monetary gain and the like, so as to keep friend and companion from distancing themselves from him. And especially Torah scholars must be very careful, just as they must be careful in all their affairs - all the more so must they be careful in this, for if they cause money to be taken from one to give to another through legal argument by means of their arguments, the man who is found liable in judgment shall not be able to restrain himself from speaking disparagingly of the Torah scholar, for "the blood is the life" (Deuteronomy 12:23). And it turns out that he transgresses "before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block," and also the severe sin of desecration of the Name is attached, and especially if the presiding judge is a proper halachic authority, and the Torah scholar digs a tunnel with many arguments and dialectical reasonings to find the innocent party liable - this matter is a consuming fire and a flame of division that rises up and brings forth a great sword (as I shall write under the entry "Mishpat and Din").
Pele Yoetz 98:2: Therefore the Torah scholar who fears the LORD, even if they gave him all the treasures of the world, shall not enter this fray, and those who seek the LORD shall not lack any good. However, there are circumstances where it is impossible to say he shall be acquitted of taking on a power of attorney - such as if his father and brother go to the Land of Israel and leave their affairs in the hands of others, and he must oversee their business and their assets, for who shall be more concerned for them than he? And even if a stranger goes to the Land of Israel and has no relatives to rely upon and cannot find a worthy man to oversee his affairs, in a place where there are no [other suitable] men, an obligation rests upon him to perform such a great kindness to bring merit to a Jewish soul who goes to the Holy Land. But if he can, let him stipulate that he does not accept to go out to quarrel and litigate case after case with others, but only that he will strive to oversee his affairs, to the extent of his ability, in peace and in a straightforward manner.
Pele Yoetz 98:3: And likewise, to be a guardian over orphans' assets is a great mitzvah, following in the ways of the Holy One, blessed be He, who is the Father of orphans, and there is no need to be concerned about anything if he must go to litigate on their behalf, for even one who takes property through litigation upon litigation to increase and improve [an orphan's estate] is saved from the demon of the poor, from the cry of orphans, and all who come to the gate of his city shall praise his deeds in the gates, that he is a good overseer of orphans' assets, as is proper to do. And this mitzvah rests especially upon the heads and leaders of cities, that their eyes be very open regarding orphans' assets, lest the capital be depleted, God forbid, and let them press the widow with pleasant speech that she withdraw all that she needs from what is hers and content herself with a minimal expenditure, with hardship and pain, so that there be an enduring fund for them when they grow up, and let them go down to judgment with anyone, whether in Jewish courts or in gentile courts, and compel them with all manner of coercion so as not to allow even a small perutah of their assets to be lost - and there is no sin or cause for suspicion in this, but rather a mitzvah and a desirable thing. And even for an adult who lacks understanding, who does not know his right from his left, and people wish to oppress and rob him - in such a case it is a great mitzvah for whoever has the ability to rescue the oppressed from the hand of his oppressor. And of this they said (Proverbs 31:8[adapted]), "open your mouth for the mute." And these matters have a measure and a limit, and between good and evil one should neither add nor subtract.
Pele Yoetz 99:1: Conformity - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shemot Rabbah 47:5): she who goes to a place shall go according to its custom. And so people say: wherever you go, do as you see done. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 50b): a person should not deviate on account of dispute, and whoever deviates has the lower hand. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 17a): a person's mind should always be mingled with people's - he should not rejoice among
Pele Yoetz 99:2: those who weep, nor weep among those who rejoice; he should not sit among those who stand, nor stand among those who sit. The general rule of the matter is: whatever they do there, he shall do, provided there is no hint of prohibition in it. And there are commonly found people lacking knowledge, who are neither versed in Torah nor in proper conduct, who, when they go to visit a sick person whose household is grieved over him, increase there words of jest and frivolity; and likewise when they go to the cemetery where the relatives of the deceased are in mourning and suffering the pain of the bereaved, and those engaged in the burial increase there eating, drinking, jest, and frivolity. And likewise there is sometimes, in a small town, a wedding where these ones weep and cry out bitterly over their own trouble, while those others raise a voice of joy and a voice of gladness of merriment and revelry, a joy of mere permission - and these erring, senseless people do not know that what they do is like thorns in the eyes and like pricks in the sides of the grieving, adding to their pain, their sorrow, and their sighing, causing their teeth to grind. And it is a common saying among people: "whoever has misfortune shall weep, whoever has good fortune shall rejoice" - but this is not fitting nor proper for us, the people of Israel, for we are brothers, like one man, like one body, and just as when there is a wound on the foot the whole body feels the pain, so it is our obligation and so it is fitting for us, that we all feel and our hearts ache over the suffering of every single one of Israel, and that we rejoice when there is joy for one person. And in any case, even if his heart does not ache, it is proper conduct to show sadness and grief, so that it be half a comfort to the one sitting in distress, seeing that others grieve over his trouble. And likewise it is not fitting for a person to tell of his sadness and his trouble at a wedding celebration and in a place of joy and at a time of gladness, but rather he shall greatly conceal his trouble and rejoice with those who rejoice, even if not in his inner heart. This is the way of wise and understanding men.
Pele Yoetz 100:1: Letter Vav: Generosity - Generosity is a good trait, when one is generous with his money for a matter of mitzvah, to perform charity and acts of kindness and all the mitzvot in their proper form. And for the well-known this needs no proof, and the whole world believes that whoever spends money for a matter of mitzvah lends to the LORD with interest at a rate of a thousand to a hundred and more - a thing without limit - and enjoys the fruits in this world, wealth and honor, with the principal remaining for the World to Come. But at the time of the deed, one does not act this way, for the nearby inclination hardens his heart and covers it in darkness, so that he does not see that "according to the abundance of the deed, if he adds, they add to him, and if he diminishes, they diminish for him" - and what fool would withhold his hand from spending another's money, since He [God] commanded it and counts it a mitzvah for him and multiplies good for him? This is comparable to what people say: "the masters give, the servants weep." This is nothing but an evil heart, for the inclination toward money is as fierce as Azazel and as hard as iron, and not for nothing did they say (Eruvin 65b), a person is recognized by his purse - for the man whose eye is evil regarding his money shall be lacking, and shall withhold himself from every mitzvah and every good trait, and shall transgress against his own mind and the mind of his Maker, and his evils and his sighs shall multiply, and his years shall be consumed in vanity, and he shall be led to the grave, and his end shall be disgraceful. Not so the man whose eye is generous - he shall run to every mitzvah with love, and shall dwell with every person in brotherhood, and shall increase the honor of his house, and his resting place shall be honorable; happy is he in this world, and it is well with him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 100:2: And it is true that the trait of generosity, like all traits, is such that some the LORD has graced with a good nature - this is a gift of God - and some have a bad nature and temperament, and their hands are bound and they cannot control even their own money for themselves - this is a bad, sick trait (as is known from the story brought in the book "Kav HaYashar" about a rich man who was scrupulous about the mitzvah of circumcision - see there). But a person who has found wisdom has the power to bring himself out of his own confinement; with counsel and stratagem he shall wage war, and little by little drive out the unclean spirit. And for this let him pray to the Former of his soul, that He save him from his distress, and "according to the pain, so is his reward," and "whoever comes to purify himself is assisted" (Shabbat 104a).
Pele Yoetz 100:3: And behold, whoever recognizes in himself his own bad trait, that he is stingy and his eye is evil, and likewise regarding any bad blemish and erring opening - this is a good sign found in him, that his heart trembles within him, and there is hope that he shall repent. And likewise one who studies books and hears the teachers shall in the end grow wise and strengthen himself to keep the straight ways of the LORD. And if at times his inclination and his nature overpower him and strangers take a stand [within him], he shall return again and lift up his head according to the Torah and by the counsel of its officers. But the evil inclination is clever - whoever errs after it does not grow wise; it is smooth from the oil of its palate, and makes a man content with his lot, thinking he has already fulfilled his obligation, while his way is against the LORD, and his palate shall not utter the true teaching, and he shall not heed the voice of his rebuker, nor shall the wicked forsake his way. But the man who desires life shall cling to the Torah and to those who study it, for its deeds are great, for it gives life to those who perform it, and writing brings him back to good, and hearing teaches knowledge and brings forth salvation. And this is a great principle, a stronghold and a tower, for every trait and for every order of service - let him know for certain, is not faithfulness good, for great is his obligation to perform his service according to his understanding and his ability, as much as he can bear. And the man who has wealth and riches in his house, according to them shall he render his redemption, and they shall come and tell of his righteousness. And whoever's hand has found abundance, and where has God led him - "according to the camel is the burden" (Ketubot 67a) - and even if he multiplies mitzvot like a pomegranate and performs wonders of charity with his money, he shall surely be punished, as the King of judgment shall impose upon him, if he does not act according to what is just, and he shall be called "wanting," for that which he should have done, he did not do. And the well-known story of the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon (ibid. 66b) is astounding to contemplate, and who is it whose heart dares say, "I have merited and fulfilled my obligation"? Therefore the obligation of the man who dwells in the shadow of the Almighty is that he do whatever is in his power to do, and let him always consider himself as one still in debt, even if he is like our teacher Moses, and let him add his hand to bring an offering - perhaps He shall be pleased.
Pele Yoetz 100:4: However, regarding generosity for a matter of mitzvah, every man can fulfill his obligation and say "I have earned merit through it," for the matter has a set measure: one-tenth - this is the straight path. And one-fifth - this is an abundant measure; whoever does this shall never be ashamed nor ever be moved. And there is a generosity that is bad, an inferior trait - such as one who is generous with another's money, and increases expenditures without his knowledge and without his permission. And even if his fellow appointed him as an agent to make some expenditure from his money, in any case such matters have a measure, and one must learn and get to the bottom of his fellow's own mind, and not squander what belongs to your fellow as you would your own. And we learned (Avot 2:12): let your fellow's money be as dear to you as your own. And in any case, he should not be overly stingy beyond what his fellow's own mind would find agreeable to be treated this way. And the same law applies to a communal treasurer, that he should not be excessively wasteful, nor should he be overly stingy, for he sins and it is not even to his own benefit - rather, he shall manage his affairs with judgment according to the matter, the place, and the time. All such matters require understanding to conduct oneself properly, without addition or subtraction. And likewise, if he must make expenditures for his own needs and the needs of the members of his household, and his own hand is limited, it must be done in proportion. And if he has the means, he shall do well for himself and increase the honor of his house, and eat and drink and clothe himself according to his standing, each man according to his own blessing.
Pele Yoetz 100:5: And the trait of generosity within the home is greatly needed, and it is a diamond decree for the matter of peace, and a precious stone for the matter of love. How good is generosity for all who possess it - it establishes peace between a man and his fellow and between a man and his wife, and drives away quarrel and enmity, and "love covers all transgressions" (Proverbs 10:12), and also "a man's gift makes room for him" (ibid. 18:16), and no evil shall befall him, and no plague shall come near his tent (Psalms 91:10). And sometimes the trait of generosity gives life to its possessor and saves him from distress and anguish - how good is its portion, no man knows its worth. But the stingy man's vessels are evil - bad toward Heaven, bad toward people, bad toward his household, and bad toward himself - and friend and companion distance themselves from him, and he shall have no peace in his own home, for he increases dispute and quarrel, and causes a soul to sin, and they shall take his money against his will, and evil shall not depart from his house, and he shall be despised and disgraced, poor and thin, and shall hand over his own soul to death, and shall descend lower and lower.
Pele Yoetz 100:6: Go out and learn what they said in the Yerushalmi: that it is forbidden for a person to greatly restrict the expenditure of the members of his household against their knowledge and will, in order to increase charity and good deeds, for this shall not find favor before the One who dwells on high, since their lives take precedence. Provided only that he not add or increase excessively in spending on food, drink, and embroidered garments, and similar things of no substance, which are vanity - for he transgresses "you shall not destroy," whereas instead of casting it away to waste for no need, or for a matter of transgression, if he were to spend it on a mitzvah, how good would his portion be and how pleasant his lot!
Pele Yoetz 100:7: And well known is the saying of King David, peace be upon him, who said (I Chronicles 22:14), "and I, in my poverty, have prepared." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Yerushalmi Peah 4:2) that he restricted his own expenditures and royal pleasures until he multiplied and gathered great wealth for the building of the Temple. And the Torah has mercy on the money of Israel, to the point that they said (Ketubot 67b) that whoever wishes to be extravagant with charity should nevertheless not give away more than a fifth, lest he become poor - all the more so for an optional matter, or to pour out and cast away to waste in the manner of the wealthy of the people who have found abundance. If only they were wise, they would understand this: that with what they cast away to waste, in demeaning work, they could have gladdened the hearts of the lowly and wretched and revived the spirit of the downtrodden. And even if they give abundantly, it is not because of this that the poor have become rich, and their houses are still empty and lacking every good thing - and if the rich were to give them their own surplus, and what appears ugly in their own eyes, to the poor man it is praiseworthy and glorious, and what to the rich man is refuse, to the poor man is choice and dear as the pupil of his eye. And this comes from the counsel of the evil inclination, which shows him that it is a shame and a disgrace to give such trivial things - but whoever has a mind and is understanding shall take counsel with himself and consult with his Maker how, with what, when, and how much is fitting to spend, and in what it is fitting to economize, and shall conduct himself properly, in a straight way, according to what kind of person he is, in a manner that is honor to the one who does it and honor to him from mankind.
Pele Yoetz 101:1: Confession - One must be careful with confession every time it is said, not to fail even once to say it with great humility, with a bowed head, in a voice of weeping, and with tears of the heart, on condition that he not return to folly. And if these conditions are lacking, absence is better than the presence of this evil, for it is insolence and impudence and worthy of disgrace and wrath - for the wrath of the LORD and His jealousy shall be kindled, and He shall say: bring this confession to your governor, or to a man like yourself - will it please him, or will he show you favor? Woe to people for the affront to the Holy One, blessed be He - and were it not for the LORD of hosts, He would judge us like the coerced and the drunk, for "we would perish, we would be lost," God forbid. But our comfort in this matter is our own insignificance and lowliness. In any case, an obligation rests upon us to strive with great vigor with all our strength, and the LORD God shall help us. And let him picture in his mind that he stands before a King, high and exalted, awesome and terrible, whose greatness is beyond fathoming, while he himself is dust from the earth, like a fleeting breath, and he says before Him: truly I have sinned against You, thus and thus I have done - and for every detail he mentions, let it be considered as though it would have been better for him to die a thousand deaths rather than commit even a small transgression to anger his Creator. And let him also consider that he is telling his distress before his Father in Heaven, for it is evil and bitter to him that he has sinned against his own soul, and that he continues to sin and cannot restrain his hand, and that his eyes have grown dim from seeing the greatness of his own evil, and he is not distressed and does not weep over his sin. And let him consider: where shall I turn for help, and to whom shall I tell this great trouble that is mine, over the past and over the present? I have nothing but to flee from before You to You, and to hide from Your anger beneath Your wings, and I shall pour out my distress to You, for You are the portion of my lot; You shall light my lamp and illuminate my darkness (Psalms 18:29).
Pele Yoetz 101:2: And how good and how pleasant it is to say, at least once a week, the full order of confession at length, and to mention all the details of sins and iniquities, for through this he shall take to heart to turn from his way. And there is great benefit in this utterance, according to hidden secrets, to purify the blemish of the letters and the attributes, and this is one of the things through which the love of the LORD is made known, that He wished to bring merit to Israel, so that by confessing what he has sinned, he fulfills a Torah-mandated mitzvah and receives good reward - there is no palate sweeter than this.
Pele Yoetz 101:3: And it is fitting for those who fear the LORD and esteem His Name to sit alone from time to time and examine every detail of the confession one by one - which of them needs repair, and which of them requires caution and a withdrawing of the hand, to make a fence and a guard, watch upon watch. So shall he do, and let him write it down, and accept upon himself with all firmness to keep and fulfill it with all strength and not transgress - and then he shall merit to say the confession as is proper to do, and pour out his speech, seeking forgiveness, and then certainly it shall bear fruit above and be accepted to atone for him. So shall the man who desires life act, who wishes to repent, and who, being a Jew, wishes to walk in a good path - such is the obligation, and through this he shall merit and inherit good and blessing for the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 102:1: "Vayehi No'am" - "Vayehi No'am" ["and let the pleasantness be"] must be said before every good deed, whether in speech or in action, and this is our comfort in this matter, for we have become very impoverished and we do not know how to have the proper intentions in anything, for every single utterance and every single deed contains supernal secrets and secrets of secrets, and builds His chambers in heaven - and even the sages who know hidden secrets cannot grasp one part in a thousand thousand thousand of the hidden wisdom that exists, all the more so we, orphans of orphans, who know nothing but the plain meaning of things. Only this shall be our comfort: that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, have revealed to us that the power of the mitzvot of God, blessed be He, operates by inherent virtue and makes an impression above, even when performed without the specific mystical intention, provided only that he intend in general that he performs this deed to fulfill the mitzvah of his God and to give Him peace of mind, and to repair the matters at their root, for the sake of all the holy ones and for the sake of the Holy One, blessed be His Name (and I have made a fitting parable on this - is it not written in my own "Beit Tefillati" - go and see there).
Pele Yoetz 102:2: And for this let him pray before every deed and every utterance, that he say "Vayehi No'am, and establish for us the work of our hands." And although even without saying "Vayehi No'am" the mitzvah also operates above by inherent virtue, nevertheless there is a difference, for certainly one who intends is not comparable to one who does not intend - the one who intends acts more powerfully and arouses the supernal matters to a greater degree. What is this comparable to? A long rope, one end of which is on the ground in a person's hand and the other end reaches to the heavens - since the person holds one end in his hand, he thereby moves the other end; but the more firmly he grasps it and shakes it with greater strength, the more of an impression he makes and the more he shakes it above. So too in this matter: the more one intends with the proper intentions, the more he arouses arousal above, to arouse love and to unify the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah. And this is the intention of our prayer when we say "Vayehi No'am" - that the LORD establish the work of our hands in the heavens above as though we had intended all the proper intentions, and prayer bears fruit. And in this verse too there are supernal secrets in every letter and every word, and it would have been fitting for us to say "Vayehi No'am" over the very being of pleasantness.
Pele Yoetz 102:3: And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, instituted for us to say "Vayehi No'am" and sanctified it as part of the order [of Saturday night] every Saturday night, and its secret is explained in the Holy Zohar (part 1, 197) that it is to arouse mercy against the judgment of Gehinnom, that it not have power over us. Therefore it seemed proper to me to intend, in saying "and establish the work of our hands," that no mishap come forth from under our hand, and nothing improper, so that we not be liable to the judgment of Gehinnom - for this let him pour out his soul before the LORD at the beginning of the week, that he enter in peace and leave in peace and not anger his Creator through it. And so, day by day he shall utter and night to night. And it is the custom of Israel not to say the order of "Vayehi No'am" on a Saturday night when a festival falls within that week, but according to the opinion of the Kabbalists it is fitting to say it even on a Saturday night that falls during Chol HaMoed [the intermediate festival days], and so do the modest ones do among themselves privately. And even regarding necessary mundane matters, it is good to say, for the sake of a mitzvah, "Vayehi No'am," and so on - this thing produces a great benefit and effect, for by faith there is nothing in the world without a root above, and everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only for His own glory, and all of man's labor is to clarify and bring forth the light of the holy sparks, and all these matters are ancient and make an impression in the heavens, provided only that he direct his heart to Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 103:1: Gathering - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 1:4): let your house be a meeting house for the wise. And whoever the LORD has graced with spacious houses shall do this: let his house be a dwelling place at all times when the wise, or those who fear the LORD and esteem His Name, wish to gather for the study of Torah or for a matter of mitzvah, and let him not worry about the extra trouble this shall cause the members of his household to clean the houses - and "a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised" (Proverbs 31:30) if she lends a hand to her husband to do every good thing and does not spare her own effort and trouble, for her business is good and all her labor shall be sweet to her against the great good stored up for her. And likewise he should not spare the expense if it is necessary, for it shall be counted a great mitzvah for him, since through him the many study Torah. And if the merit of causing an individual to perform a mitzvah is great, all the more so is the good doubled and redoubled for causing the many to perform one. And we learned (Avot 5:18): whoever brings merit to the many, the merit of the many is suspended upon him. And when the gathering takes place in his house, the Shechinah rests in his house and blessing rests in his house, as it is written (Exodus 20:21), "in every place where I cause My Name to be mentioned, I will come to you and bless you." And I have seen men of deeds who strove to hold a circumcision in their homes in order to merit that Elijah, remembered for good, come to their house - all the more so is it fitting to strive that the Shechinah come to one's house. And although even when one person alone sits and studies the Shechinah is with him, the resting of the Shechinah for an individual is not comparable to the resting of the Shechinah for the many - there is a great difference and distinction. Furthermore, when the gathering is in his house, he too shall be attached to those performing the mitzvah, and even if he does not study with them and does not understand what they study, it is impossible that he not learn something from them - comparable to one who touches balsam, who cannot help but absorb its scent. And let a man and woman whom the LORD has graced with houses consider that they shall not take their houses with them when they die, and which house they should build to be their dwelling place for the World to Come - for by doing this they build a faithful house for the World to Come. Therefore they should not mind the trouble compared to their own rest, and every person should long for the day the gathering comes to be held in his own house, and whoever leaves his house to others for a matter of mitzvah, this is a good thing. Correspondingly, a person should not agree to hold in his house a gathering for dispute, or a session of scoffers and the like, even if they gave him all the treasures of the world, for there wickedness has found rest, and he takes a leading share of all the resulting evil in the World to Come. Woe to them, for they have repaid evil by giving support to transgressors - their own hand was first in the wrongdoing, and evil, plague, and illness shall come upon them, for the LORD shall say: this is the recompense I hoped for, for having given you houses. And this suffices for whoever has a good heart - let him flee from destruction, and despise evil and choose good, for with the measure a person measures, the LORD too shall measure, and the house of the righteous shall stand.
Pele Yoetz 104:1: Letter Zayin: Remembrance - Remembrance is a great principle in the Torah, a remedy for everything, and this is the whole of man: that he remember that he is a Jew, and that an obligation rests upon him to guard and be careful against everything evil and against any hint of prohibition, and to keep all the mitzvot of the LORD, Torah-mandated and Rabbinic, in all their finest details, with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his might - this is the general way. And let him also remember to fulfill "I have set the LORD always before me" (Psalms 16:8), and to be aroused to fear and love the honored and awesome Name, to cleave to Him at every time and every moment if he can, and to say, from time to time, arousing verses, such as "I have set the LORD," "happy is the man who does not forget You," and the like. And let him also remember all the transgressions people have grown accustomed to, which have become to them as permitted - such as the bad traits of pride, anger, envy, vengeance, grudge-bearing, and exactingness, and such as excessive eating and idle talk, evil speech, prayers and blessings said hastily and without intention, robbery and deception, and the neglect of certain mitzvot and similar evils, and, surpassing them all, the neglect of Torah study. For all of these, let him remember the punishment for these traits and transgressions and their severity, and how and what is fitting to do to fence himself in to be saved from them, and how to wage war with stratagems. And it is true that at the time of the evil inclination no one remembers the good inclination, but I have already stated above (under the entry "Preparation") that he should write it down properly and utter it with his lips, "day to day he shall utter speech" - let him remember with his mouth and not forget in his heart, and the writing is the writing of God, for sight brings about remembrance, provided he remembers to write down everything just as it was understood to him from the hand of the LORD. And let him also remember to sing praise, and not fail to read what is written down, and let it be upon his forehead always as a remembrance before his eyes.
Pele Yoetz 104:2: And likewise one must remember everything he has sinned and done wrong from the day of his existence, and let his sin be before him always, for this is beneficial so that he not become proud and so that he be despised and disgraceful in his own eyes, and also so that he strive to repair what he has perverted and fulfill the ways of repentance as much as he can bear - for let him believe that his sins, which he has sinned from the day of his existence, are set in order before the Omnipresent, not one of them lacking, and there is no forgetting before His throne of glory, and if he does not repair them he shall be destined to give judgment, and "He will not utterly acquit," but rather He acquits those who repent. Therefore let him also open his eyes to this and write down what is fitting to do according to his ability - afflictions and repairs - and not transgress.
Pele Yoetz 104:3: And let him also remember the kindnesses of the LORD, for all the good He has bestowed upon him from the day of his existence, and let him give thanks according to his ability. And how good and how pleasant it would be for him to accept upon himself to do some act corresponding to what happened to him, as a remembrance of His wonders, blessed be He, and let him be humbled and say, "I am unworthy of all the kindnesses." And it is also fitting to remember always the exaltedness of God and His individual providence. And there are many, many other good remembrances, according to what kind of person one is and according to what he needs when his inclination overpowers him - let him write everything down, and day by day he shall add knowledge, add to write, and let it be with him, and he shall read it as a fixed practice and not transgress. Only let him accept this upon himself with all firmness, with great vigor and might: that he not fail to read and remember, with mouth and heart, what is written down, day by day, or once a week, or at least once a month, and through this he shall see wonders of how good his own strength is to conquer his inclination - little by little he shall drive it out; if it is stone, it shall dissolve, and if it is iron, it shall shatter (Sukkah 52b), and he shall find the means of his own redemption.
Pele Yoetz 104:4: And there is another kind of remembrance that is greatly needed, and that is the remembrance of one's own learning. And it is true that this is a gift of God, and not every person merits it, but this is the trait of every man, that with all good, sensible traits, he shall do what is in his power to do. And we find (Berachot 38b, Pesachim 68b) that the great men of the world, masters of the Talmud, would review their learning every thirty days so as not to be shamed in the World to Come, where they say, "happy is he who comes here with his learning in hand." And we, what shall we answer after them? And if they said (Eruvin 53a), "we are like a finger in a well" [dipped only briefly] regarding forgetting, what shall we say, for we have become very, very impoverished? At the very least, an obligation rests upon us to recognize our own smallness and to review the necessary laws. And those who sit on seats of judgment and render halachic decisions in Israel should not decide or render any ruling, whether of prohibition and permission or of monetary law, except from the book, after searching thoroughly, even if the matter seems to him more obvious than an egg in curd, and likewise he should not testify regarding any legal matter by saying he saw or knew or heard, and should not rely on his memory even if it seems to him as clear as [the prohibition of] his own sister - for in this orphaned generation, memory is very often false. Therefore an obligation rests upon us that the book of the Torah not depart from our mouths for halachah and for practice. And let Torah scholars tremble before rendering halachic decisions orally, and woe to that shame if he shows shame at admitting that he is not expert in the halachah, and hastily renders a decision based on memory alone - this trait destroys everything, and "she has cast down many wounded." Would that after thorough examination in the books, a matter in its proper time, he render decisions according to their halachah and judge a true judgment. And there is another remembrance that is also necessary: to remember the favor he received from his fellow, whether little or much - let it be a remembrance between his eyes all the days of his life, to repay his kindness and hold it to his credit, and not be ungrateful. And on the other hand, it is not good to remember what his fellow did that was not good and repaid him evil, for he transgresses what the Torah said, "you shall not bear a grudge" (Leviticus 19:18) - therefore let him muster his strength to remove the resentment from his heart. And more is written on this in its place under the entry "Netirah" [grudge-bearing], and see above under the entry "Ahavat Re'im" [love of fellows].
Pele Yoetz 105:1: Immorality - Israel is holy and fenced against forbidden relations, but there are great cities, and especially cities of Edom, where the gentiles are not exacting about such matters, and there are brothels that inject the evil inclination into a person like the venom of a serpent. And because of our sins there are found empty, unattached Jewish young men, and even old men, and although their own wives are with them, "stolen waters are sweet" to them, and they pursue immorality and defile themselves with the acronym "NaShaGaZ" (a menstruant, a maidservant, a gentile woman, a harlot). Woe to a generation in whose days this has come to pass. And whoever has been overcome by a spirit of jealousy, the jealousy of the LORD of hosts, shall roar like a lion against them and pursue them with a high hand until utter destruction. And if his hand cannot reach to protest against them, let him flee from that city lest he be swept away in the iniquity of the city, for truly they said (Yerushalmi Sotah 1:5): every place where there is immorality, a plague of indiscriminate slaughter comes and kills good and bad alike. And if he is compelled to remain in the city, let him do whatever is in his power to do, and rebuke the wicked with the breath of his lips, for they said in the Holy Zohar (Shemot, page 3) on the verse (Numbers 25:4), "take all the heads of the people and hang them," and so on: the heads of the people who knew of this and did not protest were seized first, and there is no jealousy before the Holy One, blessed be He, like the jealousy for the covenant [of circumcision], and especially one who has relations with a daughter of a foreign god, as explained in the Holy Zohar and in the books of ethics. And it is fitting for a person to have within him something of the knowledge of his Maker and to be greatly jealous over this corruption. Go out and learn what happened to Pinchas, who was jealous for his God and struck down his enemies and was praised, and the LORD called him "peace" (Judges 6:24[adapted]).
Pele Yoetz 105:2: And there is a kind of immorality found among some unattached men or youths who engage in self-defilement by hand and emit seed for naught by hand, or engage in male intercourse. And this comes either from a lack of knowledge of the great severity involved, or from wicked men who commit deceptive acts - and an obligation rests upon adults to warn the young and inform them of the severity of these matters until the children tremble and are seized with fear, and through this they shall cleave to the LORD forever. And it is not fitting to rely on their own trustworthiness, for there are children who cannot be trusted, whose inside does not match their outside. Therefore, in every single city, guards must be appointed over the youths, and the teacher over his students and the father over his sons shall stand guard always, and especially in the dark of night, so that they not commit iniquity, for this is a bad, sick trait, a great impurity, causing harm to himself and to the whole community, while watchfulness and rebuke bring redemption, relief, and rescue - and it is fitting to make a fence, watch upon watch, so that we not stumble into this great transgression. And well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Nazir 2a): whoever sees a sotah [a suspected adulteress] in her disgrace shall vow to abstain from wine as a nazirite. And especially one who dwells without a wife should vow the vow of a nazirite, for wine does much, and it is written (Hosea 4:11), "wine and new wine take away the heart." And well known too is their saying, of blessed memory (Avot 3:13): jest and frivolity accustom a person to forbidden relations. And it is written (Numbers 15:39), "and you shall not go astray after your own heart and after your own eyes, after which you go astray" - for the eye and the heart are the two brokers of transgression. And it is written (Proverbs 5:8), "do not come near the door of her house" - whoever guards his soul shall distance himself from it, and shall merit to gaze upon the pleasantness of the LORD and enjoy the splendor of the Shechinah.
Pele Yoetz 106:1: Caution - The matter of caution is to be careful and to guard against everything evil and against any hint of prohibition even more than one is careful about crossing through burning fire or under a sharp sword, for it is more bitter than a thousand deaths and than the province of Gehinnom and than all the evils in the world, to transgress the word of the LORD forever and to cause distress and anger and a blemish "M-H" above and "M-H" below, and it is harder than the pains of death. Therefore the man who is God-fearing and tender of heart shall flee from a hundred gates of permission rather than enter one gate of prohibition, and shall not heed the voice of his inclination, which makes the forbidden things seem light in his eyes and seeks for him false arguments and grounds for exemption, and day by day accustoms him further to prohibitions until they become to him as permitted. And let the living take it to heart (Ecclesiastes 7:2) that in transgressing even a light transgression, he causes great evil and shows that he does not care for the honor of his Maker, since he does not strive to do His will.
Pele Yoetz 106:2: And whoever fears the word of the LORD as is fitting to fear, with a fear beyond fathoming and without end, it is fitting for him to flee and distance himself very far even from a concern or a doubt of prohibition. And in a matter where there is dispute, even if ninety-nine say it is permitted and one says it is forbidden, one must be concerned, unless the halachah has been decided and the opinion of the one who forbids has been rejected. What is this comparable to? A case where ninety-nine doctors say something does not cause harm, and one says there is danger and risk to life if one eats it - what fool would not be concerned about his opinion? Surely it is obvious that every sensible person would say, "what have I to do with this trouble, to enter into a doubt of danger? Better to sit and do nothing." And if this is so regarding temporal life, all the more so regarding eternal life and not causing distress and anger to our God, King of the universe. And this thought is beneficial to save him from all sin, and brings much redemption with it, and leads him to piety. This is the straight path for those who fear the LORD and esteem His Name, and the man who walks in his innocence, the LORD shall be with him.
Pele Yoetz 107:1: Alacrity - Alacrity is said regarding positive commandments, and its matter is to worry greatly about the mitzvah, lest perhaps he not be able to fulfill it, and from this comes "the alert hasten to mitzvot" (Pesachim 4a), for a person does not know his own time, and in a moment's respite how many hindrances, how many delays, and how many enticements of the evil inclination can occur. And whoever cherishes the mitzvah as it is fitting to cherish it, more than thousands of gold and silver and more than all the life of the World to Come, his heart burns like fire and the man shall not rest until he performs it, and is concerned about even a one-in-a-thousand chance that some hindrance might befall him - and therefore the Torah said (Mechilta, Parashat Bo, ch. 9): a mitzvah that comes to your hand, do not let it turn sour. And it is included in alacrity that if he goes on a journey, he shall prepare for himself the mitzvot that it is possible he might need in a remote circumstance during the time of their fulfillment while on the road - such as a shofar, a lulav, a megillah, and its mitzvot, wine for kiddush and havdalah, and prayer books for the festivals of the year - needless to say tallit and tefillin. Even if he goes merely for a stroll, and there is a concern, even a remote concern, that he might not be able to return, he shall take them with him, and he shall always have them ready with him. And many times it is found that whoever is alert profits, while whoever is not alert to worry about remote concerns suffers loss. And likewise it is included in alacrity to walk with alacrity when going to perform a matter of mitzvah, and more is written on this below under the entry "Ritzah" [running].
Pele Yoetz 108:1: Bringing Merit - They extolled at length in the Holy Zohar the praise that comes to whoever brings merit to another. See there and you shall see wonders upon wonders. Behold, therefore, it is good for a man to strive with his own circle of companions to bring them back to good, and all the more so is the obligation greater to bring merit to his sons and the members of his household, for the yoke hangs upon his own neck - therefore let him rebuke them with the breath of his lips, and also in writing, if the LORD has graced him with a spirit of understanding, let him write a book to teach and to benefit, and if he merits that his words benefit even one person in a thousand in some generation, it is enough for him even if he came into the world for this thing alone. And in any case, a father to his sons shall inform and command his sons and his household after him, "and they shall keep the way of the LORD." And well known is the greatness of the reward of one who brings merit to the many, which is a thing beyond which there is nothing higher, that no sin comes through him (Yoma 87a). Therefore how good it is to bring merit to Israel and inform them of the way in which they should walk and the deeds they should do. And let each man help his fellow, and say to his brother, "be strong" (Isaiah 41:6), and let us strengthen ourselves for the sake of our God. And this includes examining the synagogue's prayer shawls to see if they are invalid, and repairing them. And in all such matters, whoever brings merit to the many, the merit of the many is suspended upon him, and whoever repays his soul is a man of kindness - behold, his reward is with him, and his throne is established in kindness, greater is the one who causes to act than the one who acts himself.
Pele Yoetz 109:1: Marriage - This is a mitzvah of the father toward the son: when he reaches eighteen years of age, and at the very latest twenty, to arrange a wife for him. And well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Kiddushin 29b), that until twenty years the Holy One, blessed be He, sits and waits, saying, "when will he marry a wife?" - from then on He says, "let his bones swell." And they further said (ibid.) that once twenty years have passed and he has not married, all his days are spent in thoughts of transgression. And woe to the father who is cruel to his sons and causes them such great evil. And in such a case the son is not obligated in his father's honor, and he shall be bold as a leopard to demand, respectfully, through others, and to seek the peace of mind that would be good for his soul, for this is a great transgression for the sake of Heaven [i.e., an assertive demand justified by the cause]. And all the more so, if the son is his own master, an obligation rests upon him to hasten to marry a wife and not deal falsely with his own soul. And if he is a poor man and his means do not extend to supporting a wife and children, and because of this no one wishes to be matched with him - in any case, let him do whatever is in his power to do, and seek out some poor woman even if she brings him nothing at all, and trust in the Name of the LORD that as a reward for this He shall pour out blessing upon him. And even if she is dark and unattractive - "charm is deceptive and beauty is vain" - the mitzvah of the LORD is pure and shall help him to father sons of fine form. And if he cannot find one in his own city, let him go from city to city and from province to province, and remove the mask of shame to seek a wife, for she is the cornerstone for the fence against immorality and the order of holiness.
Pele Yoetz 109:2: And regarding a daughter too, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, commanded (Pesachim 113a): "your daughter has reached maturity, free your slave and give her to him." And happy is the man who heeds the words of the Sages. But the matter is not entirely in a person's hand, for he cannot marry her off to a base and worthless man, and he should not aim high to seek a man wealthy in possessions - rather, even if he can find only a poor man who is modest and worthy, walking innocently in the way of the good, let him hasten to give her to him, and the LORD's blessing shall make him rich. And well known too is their saying, of blessed memory (Pesachim 49a): a person should always sell all that he has and marry his daughter to a Torah scholar. And they also said (Bava Batra 110a): whoever marries a woman should examine her brothers, for most sons resemble the mother's brothers, and it is assurance for him that his sons shall be Torah scholars. And whoever's eyes are not blinded shall see with his own eyes the praise of the Torah, for "she brings her bread from afar" and increases the honor of his house and gives him a future and good hope and he shall live a life of contentment - for certainly whoever is a Torah scholar fulfills the words of the Sages who said (Bava Metzia 59a), "honor your wives," and loves her as his own body and honors her more than his own body, and overlooks transgression for the sake of peace in the home, and is not exacting within his own house and the like - how many good qualities does a Torah scholar have, and above all, that she shares in his own Torah portion! It is found how good her portion is in this world and how pleasant her lot in the World to Come. Not so one who gives his daughter to an ignorant man - even if he is rich, "his own body is not money," and sometimes that wealth is lost, and every blemish is in him, and he tramples, tears, and curses, and it is bitter for her, and bitter shall her end be.
Pele Yoetz 109:3: Behold, therefore, the man who has understanding shall see with his own eyes and his heart shall understand this - he shall not set his eyes on money, and shall choose for himself wise men who fear God, even if they are penniless in wealth, for "better a dry morsel with peace in it than a house full of feasting with strife" (Proverbs 17:1). And they also said (Yevamot 63a[?]): descend a step [in social status] to take a wife. And "whoever heeds the counsel of the wise" (ibid. 12:15) shall dwell securely. And the mitzvah of heeding the words of the Sages is fitting to shield so that their match turns out well.
Pele Yoetz 109:4: And it is true that "a wife is from the LORD" and forty days before the formation of the child a heavenly voice goes forth and says, "the daughter of so-and-so is for so-and-so" (Sotah 2a). Nevertheless, I, in my poverty, have already resolved this and similar matters, that it seems to me there are three kinds of decrees. One, that it is decreed upon him that good shall come to him and no evil shall befall him - then the good shall come to him even against his will, in the manner the commentators explained, even the Exalted One. Second, that it is decreed upon him, an evil decree, written and sealed - then there is no one to save him. Third, that it is decreed upon him that it shall come to him according to his own request and according to his own effort. Therefore one must be concerned lest he be subject to this third category we mentioned, and let him do whatever is in his power to do, and sell all that he has to purchase a good portion in his lot - "if a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love" (Song of Songs 8:7) - such is the obligation.
Pele Yoetz 109:5: And included in what has been said: if they vowed to give him a great deal quickly, and a gift, and the extent of their means, or if they do not wish to give him - he should not, on this account, delay the match or break it off, but rather let him believe in the LORD and trust in Him, that He is the One who gives to each person what is fitting for him from His own open hand, increasing measure for measure. And one hour is worthwhile if he acts promptly and is saved from transgression, which is like a sharp sword compared to a treasury of every precious vessel. And since it is known, the words of the Holy Zohar, that sometimes a wicked man's sins entrap him and he marries a wife who is not fitting for him and who is not his true match, and in the end, when the time comes to return a lost item to its owner, some are swept away without judgment, and one soul is pushed aside for another. And it has also already been stated that sometimes the decree is such that the matter depends on prayer, and according to the effort and diligence, so shall a good wife be arranged for him. And it is known that a person's worthiness and his service to the blessed Name depend largely on whether he follows his wife's counsel, and if he merited a helper, he has not merited the opposite [i.e., an obstacle] (Yevamot 63a). Behold, therefore, it is fitting to precede trouble with prayer, and let every young man and young woman who fear the LORD arrange their prayer, and let a father too pour out his soul before the LORD on behalf of his children, that their match turn out well - and for this too I have raised my hand and included it in my "Beit Tefillati," with the help of Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 109:6: And behold, regarding the matter of marital relations, it is known that it is one of the Torah-mandated mitzvot (see Ketubot 47a), as it is written (Exodus 21:10), "and her conjugal rights he shall not diminish." Therefore let a person direct himself and manage his affairs with judgment according to the Torah, as explained in the books, and review the laws from time to time. And happy is the man who is careful that his conjugal time be from Sabbath to Sabbath, after midnight - however, in this everything depends on what kind of person he is and on what he sees regarding whether his wife is eager for him, showing signs of desiring appeasement, for of this they said (Nedarim 20b) that they shall have understanding children. And in any case, he should not arouse the evil inclination within himself and should not give his strength to women. And well known is what Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote (Hilchot De'ot 4:19), that ninety-nine die from excessive marital relations and one from natural causes. And since "a wife is only for children" (Ta'anit 31a, Ketubot 59b) and the entire perfection of the offspring in traits and in knowledge depends on the time of the union and the intention of the union, therefore let a man muster his strength and his might to fulfill his mitzvah at its proper time, and let husband and wife strive in their mitzvah to think pure, meritorious, and clear thoughts, and let no foreign thought come near their minds, for it is close to being an act of licentious intercourse and their own souls become corrupted, and they beget strange children - wicked, sinful, foolish, corrupt children, with every blemish in them. And what shall a living person complain when he has bad upbringing within his own house, brought upon himself by his own sins, causing evil to himself? And this is a bad, sick trait, and a cruelty greater than those who slaughter children - and if the sons knew that he was the cause of their harm, they would cry out bitterly against him, saying, "why have you muddied us and formed us in iniquity?" And shall they bear their own sin? The father and mother take the leading share, for they are the fathers of the impurity, and the sons are not so much at fault, for since the foundation is faulty and the root is bad and the husk clings to the soul, what can that son do but sin, for the soul of the wicked desires evil, and it takes labor and toil and great effort of this kind, and perhaps he might be able to overturn his own nature and bad temperament.
Pele Yoetz 109:7: Not so the holy ones who fulfill their mitzvah in holiness and purity, as is proper to do - they eat fruits in this world, that they rejoice in their own offspring, when their fruits are holy praises, wise and understanding men, complete in traits and knowledge, full of understanding and fear of the Name - there is no joy greater than this for a man, and they shall give delicacies to their own souls for the World to Come. What can we say - the mouth cannot express the evil of a man who is not careful to sanctify himself at the time of intercourse, and great is the good for whoever is careful, both men and women, that their offspring be a holy seed, offspring of [worthy] men. Behold, therefore, let every man be careful and warn his wife and his sons and daughters and all who are subject to his authority with a great warning, and let him raise his voice like a shofar before his own household - let him not be ashamed nor embarrassed to speak of matters between a man and his wife, for the honor of God and His sanctification, and let him cry out as one crying out repeatedly, saying, "have pity on your Maker and on yourselves and on the souls of your own offspring, and be very careful; be strong and courageous to sanctify yourselves at the time of intercourse."
Pele Yoetz 109:8: And let the living take it to heart (Ecclesiastes 7:2), at that time: my intention is to fulfill the mitzvah of my Creator specifically, and not for my own pleasure - rather, all my deeds are to repair the matters at their root in the upper place, for these matters are ancient. Happy is the one born of woman who merits to act to repair matters that stand at the height of the world - and He who is holy and whose servants are holy watches for when the drop shall come from which the righteous one shall be formed, as they said (Niddah 31a) on the verse (Numbers 23:10), "and who has counted the dust [rova, seed] of Jacob." And would that my own offspring be a holy seed! Or let him say aloud, so that his wife too shall hear and also set her own mind to this: Merciful Father, give me a holy seed, offspring of [worthy] men resembling Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and so on, and Rabbi so-and-so
Pele Yoetz 109:9: and Rabbi so-and-so. And let him intend that he fulfills the mitzvah in accordance with their own mind and their own intention, relying upon them. And let him consider that his union with his wife in this manner is comparable to giving over his own soul to death for the sanctification of the Name.
Pele Yoetz 109:10: And it is known that one must wash one's hands before intercourse if it has been an hour [since last washing]. And how good it would be that after washing his hands, he arrange his prayer before his union and say, "for the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah," and so on - and with the help of Heaven I have included this too in my "Beit Tefillati." And they, of blessed memory, wrote that it is good to intend at that time with the combinations of the Divine Name "Shaddai." But I say that it is good to intend the verse "Shema Yisrael" with all its intentions, and the passage "Ve'ahavta." Let the wise man hear and add learning, going deep and rising high to love the LORD and cleave to Him. And let him also instruct and teach his wife to make for him, before intercourse, the signs that Jacob gave to Rachel - namely, that she hold for him his right foot with her right hand, and her right ear with it - and afterward let him approach his wife in holiness and with great modesty, according to the law and the halachah. And after intercourse let them return and wash their hands, and let clear water be poured around his bed - this is the straight path to bring forth proper, healthy seed. Such and similar matters let every man be careful of and warn his own young men about, and happy are his children after him.
